cells.tense: You are at the far end of something you understand, and what you understand is still warm in your hands.
cells.ask: Take one thing you understand well and write down the next question it opens. Put the page where you will run into it again.
cells.core:
You can see the whole shape of something. Not pieces, not one angle — the thing as it actually is, and that doesn't leave you alone. It changes what you want to do next, which is the point of it.

You have understood something well enough that little is left to find in it, and it turns out that is not a dead end. What you understand is free to feed the next thing. Most people stop at the moment of understanding and stay there, satisfied. You likely won't, because the understanding is already pulling at something ahead of it. When the pull shows up, follow it instead of framing the insight on the wall.
cells.sheetLine: You see a thing whole, and what you see asks to be used.
cells.verb: seeing a thing whole and letting that change what you do next
cells.place: the room where what you are becomes visible in what you make

cells.tense: You are writing the ending before the middle has happened, bracing for a conclusion you don't have yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you have already decided how it reads. Say out loud, to no one, that you do not know yet — then leave it unnamed for a day.
cells.core:
You want the whole picture so badly that you keep arriving at the end of it before it gets there. A conversation starts and you have the last line ready. A week begins and you have written its last day. The clarity you reach for isn't seeing — it's pre-writing, and the present keeps having to catch up to a version it didn't agree to.

That pressure is the opposite of understanding. It keeps you braced instead of here. The way back is the smallest possible thing: let one moment be unframed. Not the whole life — one conversation, one afternoon, one question you don't answer in advance. The person in it with you may turn out different from the one you finished writing.
cells.sheetLine: You have written the ending. The moment hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: seeing a thing whole and letting that change what you do next
cells.place: the room where what you are becomes visible in what you make

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door already behind you, and the room back there has your attention.
cells.ask: Open one folder, project or draft you finished and ask one person whether it opened anything. Do not ask whether it was any good.
cells.core:
You understood something fully, at the time, and you haven't let it move you into the next room. Not that the understanding was wrong. It went in and nothing came out. The completion happened and you are still treating the thing as unfinished, because finishing and moving turn out to be two different things.

A finished thing is sitting there like an open tab. Nothing about it is asking to be reopened, and yet it holds your attention while the next thing waits. That is a room you know how to stay in. The way out is smaller than a decision: use what you understand on one piece of outside matter. One file, one conversation, one thing that takes an hour, where the understanding is the input rather than the exhibit.
cells.sheetLine: You understand it. You stopped letting it change anything.
cells.verb: seeing a thing whole and letting that change what you do next
cells.place: the room where what you are becomes visible in what you make

cells.tense: You are already reading things clearly and acting on it, while calling the read the work, the moment or the timing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you read clearly that you have been calling obvious. Say it out loud as your call, once, without hedging it.
cells.core:
You are reading situations better than almost anyone around you. A pattern forms and you can already tell where it is heading. You call that being realistic. You call it obvious. But the read is yours, and you have been handing it to circumstance — it was the timing, it was the data, anyone would have noticed.

Anyone would not have. The pattern was yours to catch and yours to name, and somewhere it feels safer to let it look like the room's rather than yours, because if the read is yours, being wrong is also yours. It isn't going to stop being yours. The way back is just admitting it. Then what you already read can serve the thing ahead instead of disappearing into the background.
cells.sheetLine: You read it clearly. You just won't sign it.

attempts.check: Rule 4 risk: the Balanced core says what the person's clarity is FOR here (completion flowing into more seeing), which the record gives as Clarity's own face but not as a claim about any individual's life — I keep it as an offer, not a verdict. A reader could reasonably say 'I am not done understanding this, the seeing is not total,' which is why no cell claims completion happened; each describes the capacity at the edge it is currently running. The asks survive a wrong read because each is one visible act — writing a question, letting a thing sit unnamed, opening the folder, using one word — that is useful whether or not the read lands and never makes anything conditional on obeying it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the diagonal's 'you have already decided how it reads' — if the person says no, that sentence is the one to drop, and the ask still stands.
